title: My 12-year-old learned to ship games with Claude
author: imonetize
selftext:
My 12-year-old son recently shipped his first game.

It is not a toy project in the sense of “draw a button and print hello world.” It is a playable chess variant called *King's Gambit*, where each chess piece has a special ability: the king can awaken after all pawns are gone, rooks can respawn once, bishops can command other pieces, knights can chain-capture, and pawns can jump like checkers.

The game has a GitHub repo, a GitHub Pages deployment, a README, version history, mobile support, sound effects, visual effects, and a basic AI opponent.

He built it with AI assistance.

I did not create the repository for him. I did not push the code for him. I did not write the README. I did not deploy it. He did the whole loop himself: idea, code, debug, commit, push, deploy.

Mostly from a phone.

His workflow is simple:

Think of a feature. Describe it to Claude. Read the code Claude gives back. Modify it. Run it. Hit a bug. Ask again. Fix it. Push to GitHub. Ship.

Then repeat.

The part that surprised me was not that AI could write code for him. That part is now obvious. The surprising part was how quickly he developed a working engineering habit around it.

After a while, he started coming to me and saying:

“Can you check this with GPT?”

He writes with Claude, then asks me to cross-check with GPT. Nobody taught him that. He figured out on his own that you should not trust one model completely, and that a second model can be useful as a reviewer.

That is a more mature instinct than many adults have with AI.

# The limit was not ability. It was rate limits.

At first he used Doubao, a Chinese AI assistant. Then he moved to Claude.

I gave him my spare Claude Pro subscription.

For most adults, $20/month is plenty. For a 12-year-old who comes home from school and immediately starts building a game, it was not. He would hit the message limit within about two hours.

I watched his usage for a while. He was not wasting prompts. He was not roleplaying or chatting randomly. Every conversation moved the game forward: implement this rule, fix this bug, refactor this part, make the AI opponent less stupid, improve the mobile layout, add a sound effect, make the capture animation feel better.

Then the limit would hit, and he would stop.

The next day, the loop restarted.

That bothered me.

Not because the subscription was expensive. Because the limiting factor had become access, not motivation.

A kid coming home from school and choosing to build games instead of scrolling short videos is rare. I did not want to throttle that.

# So I gave him a bigger machine.

I had been testing a few AI API relay services. I also had an idle VPS.

So I set up a small web-based chat interface for him. The frontend looks similar to a normal AI chat app. The backend routes to a Claude model through the relay. I locked the environment down to what he needed and gave him a URL.

It took about 30 minutes.

Now he opens the browser on his phone or computer, types in the URL, and starts coding. No daily “you are out of messages” wall. No waiting until tomorrow. No “come back later.”

If he breaks something, we reinstall. If the code is wrong, he debugs it. If he cannot debug it, he asks another model to review it. If the deployment fails, he redeploys.

The worst case is not very bad.

That changed my thinking. For adults, AI is often a productivity tool. For a child, it can be closer to a workshop.

A workshop is not safe because nothing can go wrong. A workshop is useful because things can go wrong at a scale the child can recover from.

# This reminded me of a story from 1984.

On February 16, 1984, during a microelectronics exhibition in Shanghai, a group of teenagers demonstrated computer programs on Apple II machines. One of them was a 13-year-old boy named Li Jin.

His program showed Chinese and English messages, an animated robot, and a rocket marked “Made in China.”

Deng Xiaoping stopped behind him. His scheduled stop at the booth was supposed to be short. He stayed longer, watched the demonstration, and said a sentence that later became famous in China. The exact wording is debated, but the meaning was simple:

Start with the kids.

A few months earlier, the physicist C. N. Yang had told Deng that in America, teenagers were writing software and building important things with computers.

Deng’s reply was roughly: China has many good kids. For software, we have the conditions. We need to think long-term, or we will be too late.

Replace “software” with “AI,” and the sentence still works.

Li Jin later went to Tsinghua University while still in high school. He finished undergraduate and master's coursework quickly, earned his PhD young, and eventually became part of Microsoft Research Asia.

But the most interesting part of the story is not that a talented kid became successful. It is that an adult saw a kid doing something unusual with a machine and did not say, “He is too young.”

He said, in effect, let him continue.

# The machine changed. The pattern did not.

In 1984, the machine was an Apple II.

In 2026, for my son, the machine is a phone with Claude.

In 1984, a child could print a sine curve, animate a robot, or write a small program. In 2026, a child can describe a game mechanic, generate code, run it, debug it, push it to GitHub, and deploy it for the world to play.

The feedback loop is almost zero.

That matters more than most people realize.

When I learned programming, you could be stuck for days on a small error. You needed a book, a teacher, a forum, or a more experienced friend. The cost of being stuck was high.

For my son, being stuck is part of the loop. He hits a bug, asks Claude, tests the answer, asks GPT to review it, compares the suggestions, changes the code, and runs it again.

This is not the same as being taught programming in the traditional way.

It is closer to apprenticeship with an infinitely patient but unreliable assistant.

That unreliability is important. The model makes mistakes. It sometimes overcomplicates things. It sometimes breaks working code. It sometimes invents an explanation. My son has already learned that AI output is not truth. It is a proposal.

You still have to run it.

You still have to test it.

You still have to decide whether the result works.

# I worry less about “AI dependence” than I expected.

The standard parental instinct is restriction.

Restrict screen time. Restrict tools. Restrict mistakes. Restrict access until the child is “ready.”

I understand that instinct. I still think boundaries matter. But I also think many parents confuse access with passivity.

Watching videos for three hours is passive.

Building a game for three hours is not.

When my son uses Claude to code, he is not outsourcing all thought. He is directing, testing, rejecting, modifying, and shipping. He is also learning the shape of software: files, commits, bugs, deployment, regressions, user experience, performance, mobile layout, documentation.

He does not know all the formal names yet.

But he is encountering the real objects.

That seems valuable.

I do not think every 12-year-old should be given unlimited access to every AI tool. Children are different. Context matters. Supervision matters. But I have become convinced of one thing:

If a kid is genuinely trying to build, the adult’s job is not to stand between the kid and the machine.

The adult’s job is to make the machine recoverable.

Give them a sandbox. Give them a repo. Give them a way to break things that can be restored. Give them a second reviewer. Give them enough room to run the loop.

Then get out of the way.

# The old lesson still holds.

The lesson from 1984 was not that every child should become a programmer.

It was that when a new machine appears, adults usually underestimate how quickly children can learn to use it.

They do not wait for the curriculum. They do not wait for the official textbook. They do not wait for permission from the previous generation.

They touch the machine and start.

Forty-two years ago, that machine was a personal computer.

Today it is an AI collaborator.

My son’s game is not perfect. The code is not perfect. The architecture is not perfect. The AI opponent is not perfect. That is fine.

He shipped.

That is the part I care about.

A 12-year-old had an idea for a game, used AI as a collaborator, built the thing, pushed it to GitHub, deployed it, and started working on the next version.

In 1984, the advice was: start with the kids.

In 2026, I think that advice is still right.
